questions.q: Why does this chapter use SQLite instead of a real SQL Server instance for the Load step?
options: SQLite is required by pandas
AdventureWorks2012 cannot accept writes
SQLite is a real, serverless, built-in database, so every student can follow along without running SQL Server
SQLite is faster than every other database
questions.explain: SQLite needs no server and ships with Python, making it a lighter stand-in for the warehouse target.

questions.q: What does sqlite3 require that pyodbc and SQL Server do not, to get started?
options: A separate server process running at all times
Nothing extra - it's part of Python's standard library with no server needed
A paid license
An internet connection
questions.explain: sqlite3 is built into Python and works directly against a local file, with no server to install or run.

questions.q: What does load_to_warehouse() use if_exists="replace" for?
options: To append new rows to an existing table every run
To drop and recreate the table before writing the current DataFrame
To skip the write if the table already has data
To rename the table
questions.explain: "replace" clears out the previous run's data so the table reflects only the current load.

questions.q: What is the cheap check this lesson recommends after loading data?
options: Deleting the target file and reloading it
Confirming the row count in the target matches what was expected to load
Re-running the Extract stage a second time
Printing the entire DataFrame to the console
questions.explain: count_rows() against the target is a simple way to catch load bugs before moving on.

questions.q: What would actually change if this pipeline's Load step pointed at AdventureWorks2012 instead of SQLite?
options: The entire pipeline design, including Extract and Transform
Nothing - to_sql() cannot be used with SQL Server
Only the connection/engine passed into to_sql() - the call itself works the same way
The DataFrame would need to be converted to a different format first
questions.explain: pandas' to_sql() is designed to work the same way across backends - only the engine changes.
